mcqs.question: Which of these is the best candidate for local component state?
options: A value that a sibling component also needs to read on every render
A dropdown's open/closed flag that nothing outside the dropdown ever reads
A computed total derived from two other pieces of state
Data that must persist and be shared across the entire application
mcqs.explanation: Local state is right exactly when nothing outside the component cares about the value — a dropdown's own open flag fits perfectly. A value a sibling needs should be lifted, a computed value shouldn't be stored at all, and app-wide data belongs in a shared store, not one component.

mcqs.question: In the SignupForm example, why doesn't `mismatch` need to be stored in its own state?
options: Because it never changes during the component's lifetime
Because state can only hold string values in this framework
Because storing booleans in state is discouraged for performance reasons
Because it can be computed fresh on every render directly from `password` and `confirm`, so it can never go stale
mcqs.explanation: Anything you can compute from state you already have during render is a derived value, not state of its own — `mismatch` is recalculated every render, so there's no separate copy that can drift out of sync. Booleans are ordinary state values; nothing here is about type restrictions.

mcqs.question: What's the risk of storing a value like `fullName` in state alongside `firstName` and `lastName`?
options: It can go stale if `firstName` or `lastName` update without an explicit update to `fullName` too
It uses more memory than the framework allows for a single component
It prevents the component from re-rendering when props change
It causes the component's props to become mutable
mcqs.explanation: Redundant state can only stay correct if every update site remembers to update every dependent field too — miss one and the derived value silently goes stale. Computing it inline at render time removes the possibility entirely, since there's nothing separate to forget to update.

mcqs.question: What is the main problem with syncing a derived value using an effect instead of deriving it inline during render?
options: Effects cannot access more than one dependency at a time
It permanently disables the component's ability to re-render
It costs an extra render cycle and creates a window where the derived value is briefly stale
It requires the value to be moved into a global store instead of component state
mcqs.explanation: The effect only runs after the render that changed its dependencies commits, so there's one render where the old derived value is still showing, followed by a second render once the effect's state update lands — plus a real risk of an incomplete dependency array silently breaking the sync later.

mcqs.question: What's the downside of lifting a value all the way to a page's root component instead of to the lowest common ancestor that actually needs it?
options: The value can no longer be passed down as a prop at all
Every intermediate component between the root and the real consumers has to thread it through as a pass-through prop
The framework rejects state that lives above the second level of the component tree
Local state and lifted state can no longer coexist in the same tree
mcqs.explanation: Over-lifting creates prop drilling: components that never use the value themselves still have to accept and forward it just to reach the two that do, and every one of them re-renders on unrelated changes to that value. Lifting to the lowest common ancestor confines both problems to the smallest possible subtree.
